title: & and | versus && and ||
summary: Why `&` and `|` can evaluate code you meant to skip, and how `&&` and `||` can safely stop early.
objectives: Explain why `&` evaluates both boolean sides, while `&&` can skip the right side.
Explain why `|` evaluates both boolean sides, while `||` can skip the right side.
Trace a condition to predict whether its right side runs.
Choose a safe operator and order for null checks and array bounds checks.

blocks.text: This is the exact pattern Code Coach flags:

The first side checks whether `name` is not `null`. The second side calls `name.length()`. Because the operator is `&`, Java evaluates both sides. Calling `length()` on `null` crashes. This code compiles; the problem happens only when it runs.

bad.title: Compiles, then crashes

good.title: Skips the unsafe check

blocks.note: Both programs compile. In the first, `&` evaluates `name.length()` even though `name != null` is false, so the program crashes at run time. In the second, `&&` skips the right side when the left side is false.

blocks.text: A boolean is a value that is either `true` or `false`. The operators `&` and `&&` both combine boolean values with AND: the result is true only when both sides are true. But `&` evaluates both sides, while `&&` skips the right side if the left side is false. This early stop is called short-circuiting.

blocks.caption: How `&&` protects the call to `name.length()`
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[Check name is not null]
  B --> C{Is it true?}
  C -- no --> D[Condition is false]
  D --> E[Skip the body]
  C -- yes --> F[Call name length]
  F --> G{Is length above three?}
  G -- yes --> H[Print name]
  G -- no --> E

blocks.text: The same idea applies to OR. The operators `|` and `||` both give true if at least one side is true. But `|` evaluates both sides, while `||` skips the right side if the left side is already true.

blocks.title: Check the left side first
blocks.text: With `&&`, a false left side decides the result, so Java skips the right side. With `||`, a true left side decides the result, so Java skips the right side.
Trace the flagged condition in order. The variable `name` is `null`, so the left side is false. With `&`, Java still evaluates the right side.

blocks.caption: Tracing `name != null & name.length() > 3` when `name` is `null`
rows: Java continues because `&` evaluates both sides.
The program stops before the `if` body can run.

blocks.text: Now change `&` to `&&`. The left side is still false, but now Java skips `name.length() > 3`. The whole condition is false, so the body is skipped without a crash.
The flagged code uses `&` with AND. A similar mistake can happen with `|` and OR. Follow what the left side tells Java before deciding whether the right side needs to run.

bad.title: Uses | and still calls length

good.title: Uses || and skips length

blocks.note: Here `name == null` is true. With `||`, Java skips `name.length() == 0` and prints the message. With `|`, Java evaluates that call and crashes.

blocks.text: The same safety idea helps with arrays. An array stores values in numbered positions called indexes. The first index is 0, and an array of length 3 has indexes 0, 1, and 2.

blocks.caption: `int[] values = {4, 7, 9};`
blocks.name: values
blocks.note: `values.length` is 3, but `values[3]` is outside the array. Check that an index is in bounds before reading that position.

bad.title: Uses & and reads an out-of-bounds position
bad.error: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3

good.title: Uses && to stop before the unsafe read

blocks.note: The first two checks establish that `index` is in bounds. With `&&`, Java skips `values[index] > 0` when `index < values.length` is false. With `&`, it evaluates that array access anyway and crashes.

blocks.text: For ordinary boolean values, `&` and `&&` give the same final truth value, as do `|` and `||`. The important difference is whether Java evaluates the right side. That matters when the right side can crash or should only run after a safety check.
Using a short-circuit operator is not enough if the checks are in the wrong order. The safe check must come first, so it can stop Java before the unsafe expression runs.

bad.title: Calls length before checking for null

blocks.note: The first version can crash before it reaches `name != null`. The second reaches `name.length()` only if `name != null` is true.

bad.title: Uses | for a null check

good.title: Uses || to skip the unsafe check

blocks.note: When `name` is `null`, the left side is true. `||` skips the call to `length()`, but `|` does not.

blocks.title: Compile time versus run time
blocks.text: These conditions are valid Java, so the compiler accepts them. The flagged code is not rejected at compile time. The crash happens at run time, when Java tries to call `length()` on `null`.

blocks.question: In the flagged condition, what happens after `name != null` is false?
options: Java evaluates the right side and can crash.
blocks.explanation: `&` evaluates both boolean sides. Java still calls `name.length()` even though the left side is false.

blocks.question: Which condition safely checks that `name` is not `null` and has more than three characters?
blocks.explanation: The left side checks for `null` first. If it is false, `&&` skips the call to `length()`.

blocks.question: When does `||` skip its right side?
options: It never skips the right side.
Only when both sides are true.
blocks.explanation: When the left side of `||` is true, the whole OR condition is already true. Java skips the right side.

items: `&` evaluates both boolean sides. `&&` can skip the right side when the left side is false.
`|` evaluates both boolean sides. `||` can skip the right side when the left side is true.
The flagged code compiles, but crashes at run time because `name.length()` runs when `name` is `null`.
Put the safety check first: `name != null && name.length() > 3`.
Use short-circuiting when the right side is only safe after the left side has been checked.
